item.title: Colorado football opens practice to fans and reporters, but treats it like a classified Pentagon briefing
item.description: Deion Sanders opened Colorado football practice to fans but banned all phones, cameras, notepads, and any reporting of what was observed on field.
item.content:encoded:
Colorado opened its doors to football fans on Wednesday to get a sneak peek at the 2026 roster ahead of the upcoming season, but don't expect to see any highlights or practice reports from local media and those who were in attendance.

Besides some casual talk around the water cooler, anything related to Wednesday's practice in Boulder was apparently being guarded like the codes to the nuclear football.

When Deion Sanders announced that the Buffaloes would open practice to supporters and media members, the invitation came with a lengthy list of caveats designed to prevent other programs around the country from getting intel on what Coach Prime has up his sleeve for the 2026 season.

NCAA HAS NO PLANS TO SURRENDER, AS ELIGIBILITY LAWSUITS FOR 2022 CLASS TURN INTO AN ALL-OUT LEGAL WAR

"This practice is open for viewing purposes only. It is closed for all reporting, recording and documentation purposes," Sanders mentioned in an email sent to reporters. "Nothing observed at practice may be reported, published, posted, broadcast or otherwise shared in any form, on any platform, at any time."

And, the school wasn’t messing around with the secretiveness of the open practice for those who either received a ticket or media members in attendance.

The list of prohibited items is on the same level as attending a standup comedy set from Dave Chappelle, with the school checking a number of boxes.

If fans thought they could bring in an old-fashioned pencil and notepad, think again.

Colorado wasn't allowing those, either.

That meant the only way someone could remember the depth chart, personnel groupings or key moments was by relying on a brain capable of collecting a whole lot of information in real time.

Even then, they could not report it.

"No note-taking of any kind — written, typed, dictated or otherwise," the school emphasized. "No photography, videography, audio recording, sketching or diagramming. No live coverage, live posting or real-time updates of any kind."

Before entering the open practice, fans were told they would have to leave their phones with attendants at the gate, with devices returned after the event.

Sure, there were some folks on social media complaining about having to leave their cellphones behind, but the overall reaction appeared mostly positive from fans who claimed tickets before the event eventually sold out.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHES ON HOT SEAT: BILL BELICHICK, MIKE NORVELL AND OTHERS FACING MAKE-OR-BREAK 2026

For media members in attendance, however, this was essentially a non-reportable event.

"We are on the practice field, where we got to be for all morning. Got to watch two hours of practice, but we cannot talk about any of it because that's the restrictions we have," Brian Howell of BuffBlitz.com noted.

Before the open practice, Colorado's staff made sure reporters knew exactly what was reportable:

Nothing.

"If you are uncertain whether something is reportable, the answer is that it is not," the school emphasized in the email to media outlets. "When in doubt, contact the Athletic Communications Office before publishing anything connected to this practice."

But here's the thing: This was actually a positive development for those who cheer for or cover Colorado football.

And fans can just check out the social accounts of Deion Sanders Jr. if they want to see highlights from the actual event.

Most programs only allow media members to watch certain portions of practice, which usually consist of stretching, a few individual drills and quarterbacks throwing against air.

So don't overreact to the restrictions put in place by Sanders.

If anything, he deserves some credit for opening the doors to fans and reporters who cover the team on a daily basis. Most college football coaches act as though they're giving away state secrets by allowing members of the press to watch more than 20 minutes of an actual practice.

Heck, Nick Saban was so protective of his Alabama program that nearby apartment residents with views of the practice field faced restrictions on disclosing what they saw.

Yes, college football coaches take this stuff seriously.

Look, this is pretty standard. We understand what we're allowed to discuss regarding a practice or situation we see transpire on the field.

If someone wants to risk the punishment for breaking the rules, that's on them. But running to your followers on the message board or posting tidbits of information you know are forbidden is a conscious decision to violate the rules.

UNC WANTED THE DEION SANDERS EFFECT WITH BILL BELICHICK, ALONG WITH WINS. ITS GOTTEN SOMETHING MUCH DIFFERENT SO FAR

It might sound tedious to some, but this is standard protocol, even if it sounds pretty goofy.

"Violations of these guidelines may result in removal from the facility, revocation of credentials and restriction of future access for the individual and the outlet, consistent with CU Athletics media policies," the school noted.

So, whatever transpired on the field at Colorado on Wednesday will remain close to the vest.

Want to know how quarterback Julian Lewis looked? You'll have to wait. Curious about the secondary? Same deal.

The fans most likely had a great time and got a rare glimpse of their favorite team preparing for the season.

They just better keep what they saw to themselves.

Because what happens at Colorado practice apparently stays at Colorado practice.

item.title: Cancer warning signs may appear in DNA years before blood tests detect trouble
item.description: DNA changes in certain blood cancers may signal progression to acute myeloid leukemia or myelofibrosis years before routine blood tests detect them.
item.content:encoded:
DNA patterns could reveal whether certain blood cancers are progressing years before routine tests detect those changes, new research suggests.

A study, published in the journal Cancer Discovery by the American Association for Cancer Research, followed 30 people with myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs), a group of blood cancers in which the bone marrow produces too many blood cells.

Researchers monitored DNA in the patients’ blood and bone marrow for genetic changes, then examined whether those changes were associated with blood counts, stable disease or progression to myelofibrosis or acute leukemia.

MAN WHO BEAT RARE CANCER CELEBRATES BY CANOEING 2,000 MILES WITH HIS DOG

People who stayed stable often had stable DNA without cancer-related genetic changes. This suggests a genetically "quiet" MPN is more likely to remain stable, according to the researchers, who are based at the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute in the U.K.

Patients whose disease worsened often showed DNA changes years before routine blood tests detected progression as new groups of abnormal cells emerged and grew, according to the study.

Nine participants eventually developed acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but their disease did not progress in the same way.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

In some, MPN cells gradually accumulated harmful mutations; in others, the leukemia appeared to arise from a separate group of abnormal blood cells. Similar differences were seen in those who developed myelofibrosis.

The researchers also found that hydroxyurea, a common medication used to control blood counts in people with MPN, leaves a recognizable pattern of small DNA changes in blood cells. There was no evidence, however, that the drug causes leukemia. A similar pattern was linked to azacitidine, a drug used to treat certain blood cancers.

Three participants had "triple-negative" essential thrombocythemia, a condition generally classified as a blood cancer, yet researchers found no genetic signs of cancer in their samples.

The finding raises the possibility that some patients given this diagnosis may not have a malignant disease and may not need long-term cancer treatment.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The study was limited by its small sample size, and the findings show associations rather than establishing cause and effect.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Abhishek Chilkulwar, an oncologist with Orlando Health, noted that most people with MPNs can live with them "for decades."

The doctor, who was not involved in the study, called the findings a "striking demonstration" that DNA changes may signal the development of certain cancers a decade before diagnosis and that their future path may "already be 'written' in a patient's cells long before doctors can see any outward sign."

"More broadly, it's an early example of what could become precision medicine for blood cancer prevention, using a patient's own genetic data to predict risk years in advance, then someday intervening before disease progression rather than only treating it after the fact," he said.

"That's the direction this kind of research is pointing, even though the tools to act on it aren't fully built yet."

The results suggest that periodically retesting a patient’s DNA over time could give doctors a "heads-up" that someone’s disease is heading in a dangerous direction, "well before" it shows up in routine blood work, Chilkulwar added.

"In the near term, the realistic use of this is modest: closer monitoring, not new treatment," he said. "A patient found to have acquired a high-risk mutation could be shifted to more frequent blood counts and, if warranted, more frequent bone marrow checks. So, if progression does happen, it's caught earlier.

"It would not be a reason to start stem cell transplant evaluation; transplant is a serious procedure appropriately reserved for patients who have actually progressed to myelofibrosis or AML, not something to prepare for based on a mutation that might cause problems years down the line," the doctor cautioned.

The next step, Chilkulwar said, would be pairing early genetic detection with drugs targeting those specific mutations, potentially preventing or delaying disease progression.

item.title: Nancy Pelosi denies knowing about Biden's decline, claims those who knew 'should have acted'
item.description: Nancy Pelosi denied knowing about Joe Biden's decline but said those who did know "should have acted" sooner during an interview on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi denied knowing anything about former President Joe Biden's decline on Tuesday, but said those who did know "should have acted" on the information.

Pelosi said repeatedly she didn't know Biden had experienced any sort of decline and told Politico's Jonathan Martin, "I didn't know, but I do think that those who did know should have acted upon that information, whatever that means."

"There was the staff saying the family knew, the family saying the staff knew, I don't know," she added, noting they should have acted sooner. The pair had been feuding over the 2024 race, but Pelosi said in March that they had spoken.

JILL BIDEN SAYS SHE THOUGHT JOE WAS HAVING A STROKE DURING HIS DISASTROUS 2024 DEBATE PERFORMANCE

Pelosi, who was widely considered to be a driving force behind Biden dropping out of the race in 2024, also repeated her denial that she didn't ask the former president to drop out.

"I only said to President Biden, ‘I’ve come to question the polling that you have and how your campaign is being conducted,'" Pelosi said. "I didn't ask him not to run or anything like that. This is what I asked. 'I would hope that we could have some other pollsters come in and sit with your pollster and discuss what they hear out there.'"

"And I did say this, 'I think the public would like to hear that you've had a testing that demonstrates that you can serve the next [term],'" she added.

Martin asked Pelosi how Biden responded to her statement. The former House Speaker said Biden said he was being tested in his job daily.

JILL BIDEN CLAIMS JOE WOULD BE ‘EXCORIATED’ IF HE DID WHAT’S HAPPENING IN CURRENT WHITE HOUSE

Pelosi said, "He responded. We were prayerful, you know, Catholic. We're prayerful. We had our rosaries and all that. And we had a lovely meeting. It was only the two of us, except when he put somebody on the phone to talk about the polls. So, whatever people said about it there, didn't come from me, or maybe it came from somebody in his staff, but none of his staff was really in the room. He said, ‘I get tested every day in what I'm doing and the rest of that.’ I said, ‘I think people want to see something more in that regard.’"

Fox News political analyst Guy Benson told Fox News Digital that her latest statements came across as "non-credible gaslighting."

"Everyone with eyes and ears clocked the former president’s clear decline. The gaslighting denials came from partisan actors who were invested in a political outcome, very much including Pelosi. Once their gaslighting efforts died on that debate stage, they feigned shock at the very reality they’d cynically attacked others for noticing, very much including Pelosi. Because their desired outcome abruptly required turning on Biden, the knives came out. And the sharpest knife may have belonged to Pelosi. She can try to deny this, but it’s just more non-credible gaslighting," Benson told Fox News Digital in a statement.

Pelsoi appeared on MS NOW's "Morning Joe" in early July 2024, after Biden had assured Democrats he was remaining in the race. Pelosi insinuated in the interview that Biden was still deciding whether or not he would remain in the race.

JAMES CARVILLE ARGUES ONE KEY MISTAKE FROM BIDEN HAS LEFT DEMOCRATS IN DISARRAY

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"It's up to the president to decide if he is going to run. We are all encouraging him to make that decision, because time is running short," Pelosi said at the time.

Biden's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
